To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
(1) we can manipulate a stock price forecasting model by injecting fake tweets, (2) we can do this without modifying the training data, and (3) the attack is robust to the model architecture.

1) we show that an attacker can manipulate the output of a sentiment analysis model to forecast the price of a stock incorrectly; and 2) we show how to quantify the impact of such manipulation on the attacker's profit.

(1) sentiment analysis of Twitter posts can be used to manipulate the prediction of an ML model that forecasts the price trend of a stock and (2) the manipulation can be done by an adversary who has access to the model's prediction and who can control the tweets posted on Twitter.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the following: (1) the robustness of a sentiment analysis model to adversarial inputs at test time, (2) the potential impact of such vulnerabilities on the performance of a trading algorithm, (3) the feasibility of the attack in practice and the cost of the attack, (4) the implications of the attack for the use of ML in finance, and (5) a set of recommendations for the industry.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the use of ML in trading algorithms should be treated with the same level of caution and skepticism as the use of any other external signal.
we have shown how a machine learning system that is used to predict the future can be manipulated to predict a false future.
adversarial ML is not just a theoretical problem.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the robustness of ML models should be evaluated in settings that are representative of the intended use of the model.
ML is vulnerable to adversarial attacks, even in settings with clear incentives for the adversary and when the attack can be mounted remotely.
the robustness of ML models should not be evaluated in isolation from the system in which they are used.
